# The Event Loop: Notes From a JavaScript Learner

For a long time I wrote JavaScript without really understanding how it runs. Callbacks, promises, async/await — they all seemed to work by magic. The magic disappeared once I sat down and studied the event loop, the single mechanism that decides when every piece of my code actually executes.

## One thread, one call stack

JavaScript executes on a single thread with a single call stack. When a function is called, a frame is pushed onto the stack; when it returns, the frame is popped. If a function takes too long, nothing else can run — the page freezes. That is why long computations either get chunked, moved into a worker, or rewritten to yield back to the browser.

The single-threaded design is a simplification, not a limitation to fight. It removes whole categories of bugs: race conditions on shared memory, deadlocks between competing locks, subtle interleavings that only reproduce on Tuesdays. The price is that we must never block the stack for long.

## The queues

Around the call stack live several queues, and keeping them apart is most of the work:

- The macrotask queue holds callbacks from timers, DOM events, and I/O completion.
- The microtask queue holds promise reactions and queueMicrotask callbacks.
- Microtasks always drain completely before the next macrotask starts.

When the stack empties, the runtime finishes all pending microtasks first, then takes exactly one macrotask, then drains microtasks again. This two-level structure explains the classic interview puzzle: a setTimeout(fn, 0) callback always runs after a resolved promise callback, because the promise reaction is a microtask and the timer is a macrotask.

## Promises are a queue discipline in disguise

Before promises, we chained callbacks by hand, and every step could split into success and failure paths that drifted apart. A promise is an object that wraps a future value and hands you a thenable chain: each then registers a microtask, so callbacks run in a deterministic order regardless of when the value arrives. Async/await is sugar over the same machinery — an await pauses the async function, schedules the rest of it as a microtask continuation, and frees the stack.

The practical lesson I keep relearning: never assume ordering from how the code is written. Ordering comes from which queue each callback lands in and when the stack empties. When in doubt, I trace three things: which stack frame am I in, which queue does this callback come from, and is the stack about to drain.

## Rendering wants its turn

Between macrotasks, the browser gets a chance to render. If a microtask keeps spawning more microtasks, rendering never happens, because the microtask queue never drains. A classic mistake is an infinite chain of promises that locks the page just as effectively as a while(true) loop. The fix is to break the chain deliberately — yield to a macrotask, split the work into chunks, or move it off the main thread entirely.

## Cheat sheet

- One call stack; long frames freeze everything.
- Microtasks drain fully between macrotasks.
- Promise callbacks are microtasks; timers are macrotasks.
- Rendering happens between macrotasks, never mid-microtask-drain.

The event loop was the moment JavaScript stopped feeling like a bag of tricks and started feeling like a designed system. Every async pattern I have learned since is just a new way to hand work to a queue.
